vignette:
Keanu rarely spoke of the night the sea took his wife, Leilani. Two years on, the memory remained less a story he could tell and more a series of physical sensations that ambushed him. He and Leilani had been in a small beachfront bungalow, celebrating their twentieth anniversary. He remembers the silence first—an unnatural, deep quiet that fell just after midnight, a hush so profound it woke him. Then the low rumble, the taste of salt already in the air, and the sudden, violent roar as the world became a churning chaos of darkness, splintered wood, and water. He survived. She did not. Now, as an auditor living in coastal California, any building near the water feels like a trap waiting to be sprung. The memory itself feels alien, so extreme that he finds it hard to believe it actually happened to him, yet it governs his entire existence.

In the months that followed, waking up became a recurring trauma. Any moment of disorientation in the dark would plunge him back into the bungalow, the smell of brine and mud thick in his nostrils, the gritty taste of saltwater coating his tongue. Because the memory returned not as a story but as a raw sensory assault, anything that evoked its core elements—the unnatural quiet that preceded the roar, the smell of the ocean—became a fresh source of alarm. These vivid sensory intrusions made the night itself feel predatory, and soon, the darkness was no longer just an absence of light but a direct signal of imminent danger. This constant sense of threat, in turn, kept the memories close to the surface; sitting in his quiet office, the unusual silence would suddenly make him feel as if something terrible was about to happen, and the taste of salt would flood his mouth, immediate and visceral. The memories made the world feel threatening, and the threatening world made the memories impossible to escape.

He came to believe the world was a fundamentally dangerous place and that he was utterly helpless to protect himself or anyone he cared about. This conviction became the lens through which he saw everything. This profound sense of vulnerability meant that any novel or unpredictable situation—not just those reminiscent of the tsunami—now functioned as a trigger. Because he was certain he would be unable to handle another catastrophe, the mere fact of not knowing what to expect at a new client's office was enough to provoke a sense of imminent doom. It drove him to avoid any situation he couldn't control, a habit that began to constrict his life. He stopped going to unfamiliar places, which became a significant problem in his work as an auditor; he began making excuses to avoid site visits to new clients, claiming he could do the work remotely. His sense of helplessness also convinced him that talking about Leilani or the disaster was pointless. Instead, he began smoking again, a habit he’d quit a decade earlier. A pack a day became his shield, the chemical calm a flimsy barrier against the ever-present tension. Any trigger, like waking in the night, would send him fumbling for a cigarette on his nightstand, the flare of the lighter a small defiance against the suffocating dark.

The strategies he used to cope only seemed to dig him deeper into the hole. The more he smoked and withdrew, the more it confirmed his belief that he was broken beyond repair, feeding the profound emotional numbness that had settled over him. He felt, in his own words, "dead inside." This constant state of self-imposed isolation and nervous system agitation kept his threat perception dialled to maximum. A delayed email from a colleague wasn't just an inconvenience; it was a sign that something had gone terribly wrong. The avoidance of relaxation also had a perverse effect: because he never allowed himself to feel at ease, any accidental moment of peace—a warm sunbeam, a kind word from a stranger—felt jarring and intensely dangerous, a prelude to disaster. This made the experience of happiness itself a potent trigger, one to be stamped out immediately.

His belief in his own helplessness made every trigger feel catastrophic. A moment of joy with his son would be instantly followed by a crushing wave of guilt and the thought, "I couldn't save her, I can't save anyone," which only reinforced his feeling of being a passive victim in a hostile world. This numbness also distorted the trauma memory further, making it feel even more unreal, like a film he’d once seen. It was a closed loop of misery: the triggers confirmed his helplessness, his helplessness made him avoid life, his avoidance proved he was broken, and his brokenness made the world a terrifying place.

It was the announcement of his son’s engagement that finally brought Keanu to therapy. The thought of a wedding—an event that demanded joy, presence, and relaxation—felt like an impossible summit. He pictured himself standing there, a ghost in a suit, unable to feel happiness for his own child, waiting for the other shoe to drop. The fear of his internal emptiness being visible to everyone, or of an uncontrollable panic attack ruining the day, was more terrifying than the silence or the dark. He admitted he felt trapped, unable to move forward but terrified of looking back, and quietly asked if it was possible to ever feel safe in the world again.
